title: Messier 92 (Hubble)
caption: Globular cluster Messier 92, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Messier 92 · constellation Hercules · about 25,000 light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: NASA Hubble image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: Thousands of white stars crowd a black background in this Hubble Space Telescope image of Messier 92, or M92. It is a globular cluster, a dense, roughly round swarm of old stars held together by gravity. M92 lies about 25,000 light-years away in the constellation Hercules.

Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys recorded the cluster through two filters. NASA ranks M92 among the brightest globular clusters in our galaxy, and its stars appear here as individual white points.

NASA released the image in 2021 alongside a preview of plans for the James Webb Space Telescope, which had not yet launched. Astronomers expected Webb's infrared instruments to reveal stars hidden even from Hubble and to pick out single stars in nearby galaxies. A team led by Daniel Weisz of the University of California, Berkeley, planned an early program on resolved stars, along with free software to help other astronomers measure them.

understand.summary: Hubble's ACS took this image through two filters. NASA shows F606W in cyan and F814W in orange.
understand.eye: The colors are hues assigned to the two filters, so they are not exactly what an eye would see.

explore: Webb's planners hoped sharper measurements of individual stars would improve distances to nearby galaxies and so help with the open question of how fast the universe is expanding. Data from these early programs were to be shared with other astronomers right away through the Barbara A. Mikulski Archive for Space Telescopes.
